investigacion.base:
Nothing has been decided yet. The meeting is 11 days away, so there's no vote and the question can't resolve Yes or No on current information.

**Resolution sources**
- **FDA 2026 DODAC meeting-materials page:** My searches didn't return this page, so I can't confirm the official notice, the briefing documents or the voting questions. FDA usually posts briefing documents about 2 business days before a meeting, which would be around October 28, and posts the vote results or minutes after it. Check the page directly.
- **Metaculus FAQ:** This defines "credible sources" in the usual way (major news outlets, official records). It doesn't change anything here.

**Timeline**
- **October 23, 2025:** FDA rejected the application with a complete response letter. FDA acknowledged the STAR trial met its primary endpoint but concluded the submitted data did not support effectiveness. Sydnexis then filed a Formal Dispute Resolution Request with the FDA Office of Specialty Medicine.
- **July 2026:** FDA said it would convene an advisory committee. As of July 13, 2026, a meeting date had not been set. The CEO said the company requested it include practicing pediatric ophthalmologists and optometrists. The Pink Sheet called it the latest controversial FDA decision headed to an advisory committee.
- **September 24, 2026:** Sydnexis announced the meeting date. The FDA has scheduled an Advisory Committee meeting, including an Open Public Hearing, for October 30, 2026. The application is NDA 219694, proposed for slowing myopia progression in children aged 3 years or older.
- **Around October 2026:** Sydnexis, a private company, has just sold its European royalties for $23 million upfront to fund that fight.

**The data**
- STAR enrolled 847 children ages 3–14 across the U.S. and Europe.
- The primary endpoint was progression beyond −0.75 D at month 36. The 2003 FDA Dermatologic and Ophthalmic Drugs Advisory Committee identified this threshold as clinically meaningful, and the FDA later agreed to its use in STAR.
- Results: the 0.01% dose met the primary endpoint versus vehicle (P = .0226), and the key secondary endpoint, annual progression rate, had P = .0002.
- Safety: no new safety signals through month 48, but rates of specific adverse events, including photophobia or near-vision complaints, were not included in the announcement.
- The drug is approved in the EU and UK, licensed to Santen and marketed as Ryjunea. No FDA-approved drug for pediatric progressive myopia exists in the US.
- Support from clinicians: a Citizen Petition signed by more than 1000 eye care professionals, plus public backing from the president of the American Association for Pediatric Ophthalmology and Strabismus (AAPOS).

**Key uncertainties**
- **There may be no vote.** FDA said the committee will be asked to discuss various aspects of the company's application. That wording leaves open a discussion-only meeting, which would annul the question. The voting questions should be in the briefing documents expected around October 28.
- **FDA's reasoning isn't public.** We don't know exactly why FDA rejected the data despite the hit on the primary endpoint. Possibilities include the modest effect size, how robust the result is, or the fact that only one of two doses worked. The FDA briefing document will show this and will be the biggest signal before the meeting.

**Base rates** (from my general knowledge, not checked against the searches)
- Historically, roughly 60–70% of FDA advisory committee votes come out in favor.
- Advisory committees convened over a disputed rejection, where FDA reviewers argue against approval, have more mixed results.
- Panels that include practicing clinicians, with strong unmet need and an existing EU approval, tend to lean favorable.

**Scheduled events**
- Around October 28: briefing documents and voting questions posted.
- October 30: the meeting, open public hearing and any vote.

**Prediction markets:** None showed up in my searches.

**Current status:** No vote has happened, so the question is unresolved.

criterios: This question resolves YES if, at the Dermatologic and Ophthalmic Drugs Advisory Committee (DODAC) meeting held on October 30, 2026 to discuss NDA 219694 for Sydnexis's atropine sulfate ophthalmic solution 0.01% (SYD-101), the committee takes a formal vote on a question asking whether SYD-101's benefits outweigh its risks (or, equivalently worded, whether the committee supports approval/marketing of SYD-101 for the proposed pediatric myopia indication), and more members vote "Yes"/in favor than vote "No"/against. It resolves NO if more members vote "No"/against than "Yes"/in favor, or if the vote is a tie. Resolution is based on the official voting results posted by the FDA in the meeting materials/minutes for this meeting at https://www.fda.gov/advisory-committees/dermatologic-and-ophthalmic-drugs-advisory-committee/2026-meeting-materials-dermatologic-and-ophthalmic-drugs-advisory-committee or as reported by [credible sources](https://www.metaculus.com/faq/#definitions). Abstentions are not counted as "Yes" or "No" votes.
letra_pequena: If the committee holds more than one formal vote, the question used for resolution is the one most directly addressing overall benefit-risk balance or support for approval/marketing of SYD-101 for the proposed indication; if multiple such votes are taken, the one taken latest in the meeting governs. If the meeting is cancelled, postponed to a date after October 30, 2026, or the committee takes no formal benefit-risk/approval-oriented vote (e.g., it is convened only for discussion with no vote), the question is annulled. If the FDA meeting-materials page is unavailable, resolution relies on [credible sources](https://www.metaculus.com/faq/#definitions) reporting the official vote tally.
razonamientos:
(a) **Time left:** The meeting is scheduled for October 30, 2026, 11 days from today.  
(b) **Status quo:** FDA has issued a Complete Response Letter saying the submitted data did not establish effectiveness. No committee vote has occurred.  
(c) **Reference class:** FDA advisory committees often vote favorably—roughly 60–70% is a useful broad, unverified base rate—but a meeting following an FDA effectiveness rejection is a less favorable subset.  
(d) **No scenario:** Members accept FDA’s concerns about the strength or clinical significance of the efficacy evidence and vote against approval.  
(e) **Yes scenario:** Members find the prespecified endpoint, supporting secondary result, safety record, and unmet need sufficient for a favorable benefit-risk vote.  
(f) **Resolution technicality:** A discussion-only meeting, cancellation, or postponement beyond October 30 would **annul** the question, not resolve it No. If there are multiple qualifying votes, the latest governs.

The FDA’s existing negative effectiveness conclusion outweighs the positive trial result for me, though the result and European approval leave a substantial chance of a favorable vote.

Probability: 42%

(a) **Time left:** The meeting is scheduled for October 30, 2026, 11 days from now. A vote would likely be known that day, with official results posted later.

(b) **Status quo:** No vote has occurred. The FDA’s last stated assessment was that the submitted data did not establish effectiveness, despite the trial meeting its primary endpoint.

(c) **Reference class:** Advisory committees often vote favorably—roughly 60–70% is a broad, unverified historical estimate. A meeting following an FDA rejection is a less favorable subset, so I give that broad base rate limited weight.

(d) **No scenario:** Members agree with the FDA that the statistically significant result does not establish a sufficiently meaningful or robust benefit, and more vote against than for.

(e) **Yes scenario:** Members find the prespecified trial results persuasive, consider the safety profile and lack of approved US drug alternatives, and vote that the benefits outweigh the risks.

(f) **Resolution technicality:** A tie counts as **No**; abstentions count neither way. If there is no formal benefit-risk or approval-oriented vote, the question is **annulled**, not resolved No. A favorable vote would not itself approve the drug.

The FDA’s prior negative effectiveness judgment is my strongest signal, but the positive trial endpoints and apparently low safety risk leave a substantial chance of a favorable panel vote.

Probability: 44%

(a) About 11 days. The vote, if one is held, happens October 30, 2026, and the tally is usually reported the same day.

(b) Nothing has been decided. The FDA's standing position, set out in the CRL, is that effectiveness was not demonstrated. If the committee simply defers to the agency, the outcome would be No.

(c) Historically, roughly 60–70% of advisory committee votes favor the product. That rate drops, to roughly 40–50%, when the FDA review team argues against approval or the meeting stems from a disputed rejection. Low-risk drugs with high unmet need and clinician-heavy panels tend to do better than that.

(d) No scenario: the FDA briefing document stresses three problems. Only one of the tested doses worked, which breaks dose-response. The effect on refraction and axial length is small. And the case rests on a single trial with a modest p-value (0.0226). Statisticians and methodologists on the panel would then vote that benefit was not shown, and the panel would follow the FDA's framing.

(e) Yes scenario: the drug is very safe, has EU/UK approval, and the U.S. has no approved alternative. Clinicians already widely use compounded atropine, and the primary endpoint was the one the FDA agreed to in advance. Pediatric ophthalmologists and optometrists on the panel, swayed by the open public hearing, vote that benefits outweigh the minimal risks.

(f) If the meeting is discussion-only, the question is annulled, so I am forecasting conditional on a vote. One technicality matters. The FDA may phrase the vote as "has substantial evidence of effectiveness been demonstrated?" rather than as benefit-risk. Such a question would probably count as the approval-oriented vote, and effectiveness-framed votes tend to go worse for sponsors than benefit-risk votes for safe drugs. A tie resolves No.

Weighing these, the safety profile and unmet need pull toward a favorable vote, while the FDA's likely critical briefing and a possible effectiveness-framed question pull against it. I put it slightly above even.

Probability: 54%
